# [Subscriptions](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#subscriptions)

Table of contents

With a Muse Code subscription, you pay a flat monthly rate for usage of [Muse Code](https://dev.meta.ai/products/muse-code), instead of paying per token. Subscription benefits and availability may vary by region. Available benefits will be shown to you during onboarding before you subscribe.

## [About subscriptions](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#about)

To sign up for a Muse Code subscription, you will need a Meta Account. Using your Meta Account, you can create an associated Meta Model API account and sign up for a subscription. The subscription applies to the Muse Code API key that is automatically connected in the Muse Code CLI onboarding process. This credential is for use with Muse Code only. Any additional API keys you create under your Meta Model API account will be billed through [pay-as-you-go](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/auth#billing).

You must be 18 or the age of majority in your country to subscribe. Your subscription is subject to the [Meta Subscription Terms of Service(opens in new tab)](https://www.facebook.com/legal/meta_subs_terms), and your use of Muse Code and the Meta Model API is governed by the [Meta Model API Terms of Service](https://dev.meta.ai/legal/terms-of-service) and the [Meta Model API Acceptable Use Policy](https://dev.meta.ai/legal/acceptable-use-policy).

How Meta uses your content — the prompts, code, files, and context you send, plus the model responses you get back — depends on whether [Contributor mode](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#contributor-mode) is on in your settings, and is described in the [Meta Model API Terms of Service](https://dev.meta.ai/legal/terms-of-service).

There are 4 subscription plans available for Muse Code:

### [Everyday Usage](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#everyday-usage)

*   Access to Muse Spark, Muse Wonder and Muse Image
    
*   Send 10-50 prompts every 5 hours, including image and video uploads
    
*   Use voice mode
    
*   Get access to web search
    

### [High Usage](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#high-usage)

*   Everything from the Everyday Usage plan
    
*   5x more usage than the Everyday Usage plan
    
*   More multimodal inputs
    

### [Power Usage](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#power-usage)

*   Everything from the High Usage plan
    
*   Access to Muse Wonder Full, the higher-capability variant of Muse Wonder
    
*   20x more usage than the Everyday Usage plan
    
*   Early access to new features
    
*   Higher file uploads
    

### [Maximum Usage](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#maximum-usage)

*   Everything from the Power Usage plan
    
*   80x more usage than the Everyday Usage plan
    

## [Contributor mode](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#contributor-mode)

Muse Code subscriptions default to Contributor mode. In Contributor mode, you get more usage from your plan in exchange for letting Meta use your content to train future Meta models. Contributor mode is a setting in Muse Code, and you can turn it off at any time, at which point your future content is not used to train Meta models (unless you turn it back on in your settings).

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are each available in either mode on the plans that include them. For the models each plan includes, see [Muse Wonder availability](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-wonder#availability).

### [Turn Contributor mode on or off](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#turn-contributor-mode-on-or-off)

To change the setting from an interactive session:

1.  Type `/settings`.
    
2.  Under **Model**, select the **Contributor mode** row.
    
3.  Press Enter to switch it on or off. The row text changes to show the new state.
    

The change applies from your next request. Muse Code saves the setting on the computer you're using, so if you use Muse Code on more than one computer, change it on each one. On a new computer, your first interactive session turns Contributor mode on and shows a notice that says so.

Headless runs (`muse exec`) use the same saved setting. On a computer with no [settings file](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/configuration#settings-file), a headless run has Contributor mode off. If the settings file exists but the setting has never been saved, a headless run can have Contributor mode on. To control the mode of headless runs in scripts and CI, set it on every run with the flag or environment variable below.

To turn Contributor mode on or off for a single run without changing your saved setting, pass `--contributor-mode on` or `--contributor-mode off` to `muse` or `muse exec`:

bash

`   muse exec --contributor-mode off "Summarize the changes on this branch"   `

You can also set the environment variable `MUSE_CONTRIBUTOR_MODE` to `1` (on) or `0` (off) for a run. If you set both, the flag wins.

While a per-run override is active, the **Contributor mode** row in `/settings` shows **(run override)** instead of the current state. Switching the row then saves your setting for later runs, but the current run keeps the override.

The **Contributor mode** row appears only while you're signed in with an active Muse Code subscription. It doesn't appear if:

*   You're using pay-as-you-go billing.
    
*   Your account has [Zero Data Retention (ZDR)](https://dev.meta.ai/help/policies-and-privacy/zero-data-retention).
    
*   Your organization manages the setting through its managed configuration. Contributor mode then stays off, and the flag and environment variable have no effect.
    

## [Choose pay-as-you-go or a subscription](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#choose-a-plan)

Muse Code supports 2 ways to pay for usage:

*   **Pay-as-you-go**: billed per token consumed with your Meta Model API key. See [billing and plans](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/auth#billing).
    
*   **Subscription**: a flat monthly rate (see the plans above). It works only through the Muse Code CLI while signed in with your Meta Model API account.
    

If you reach your plan's usage limit, you can upgrade to the next plan, or wait until your limit refreshes. If you are on the Maximum Usage plan, you must wait for your limit to refresh. Usage through any additional API keys you create is billed pay-as-you-go.

## [Subscribe](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions#subscribe)

Sign in to Muse Code with your Meta Model API account on [dev.meta.ai](https://dev.meta.ai/), then subscribe through Accounts Center:

1.  Go to **Subscriptions** in [Accounts Center(opens in new tab)](https://accountscenter.meta.com/).
    
2.  Select **Muse Code**, then choose a plan and complete checkout.
    
3.  On success, you will see a confirmation

# Meta Muse Code pricing: what a free coding agent really costs

![Rama Adi](/_next/image?url=%2Fimages%2Fblog%2Fauthors%2Frama.jpg&w=160&q=75)

Written by

Rama Adi

![Katelin Teen](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwmeojibgfvjvinftolho.supabase.co%2Fstorage%2Fv1%2Fobject%2Fpublic%2Fwp-uploads%2F2024%2F10%2Fkatelin-profile-e1752733682107.webp&w=160&q=75)

Reviewed by

Katelin Teen

Last edited August 17, 2026

Expert Verified

![A developer at a terminal watching coins pour out of the screen into a basket marked with an infinity symbol](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn-public.eesel.ai%2F314c3443-850d-416d-8721-d2e52c7ac2e2%2F585703e2-5508-4d19-8a3a-24b54e4a1f15%2F3cf95f6763c24cfcb26b5f966f989628.webp&w=1680&q=75)

TL;DR

Muse Code costs nothing. Meta charges you for the model underneath it: $1.25 per million input tokens, $0.15 cached, and $4.25 output on `muse-spark-1.2`, or `$0.10 / $0.002 / $0.20` on the contributor tier if you let Meta train on your code. There is no seat price, no subscription, no free tier, and no trial credit anywhere on Meta's pricing, product, or billing pages. I checked all three.

That sounds cheap, and per token it is. The catch is that Muse Code decides how many tokens to spend, and nothing stops it. Out of the box it runs the expensive model, at the second-highest reasoning setting of seven, with three background observer agents each making their own model calls, and a subagent fan-out that scales to your CPU core count. Meta ships no spend cap of any kind. The only thing called a limit in the billing docs is a "payment threshold," and it goes up as you pay.

If your reason for looking at token pricing is that you want a support bill you can forecast, that is a different problem with a different answer. eesel uses 1 credit per ticket or chat, however long, on a fixed monthly price from $299/month for 500 credits, rather than billing per million tokens, which means the bill tracks work handled rather than how long a model felt like thinking. That unit is the entire point.

## What Muse Code actually charges you for

Muse Code is [Meta AI](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/meta-artificial-intelligence)'s [terminal AI coding tool](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/terminal-ai-coding-tool), shipped in beta on 5 August 2026 alongside the Muse Spark 1.2 model. You install it with one line, `curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash`, and run it by typing `muse` in a project directory.

Here is the thing that trips people up on the [Muse Code product page](https://developer.meta.com/ai/products/muse-code/): the section headed "Models and pricing" contains no price for Muse Code. It contains a five-column token table for Muse Spark. I searched the full rendered body text of that page for the words free, trial, credit, subscription, seat, plan, spend, limit and cap. Zero hits on all nine. The entire commercial story of Meta's coding agent is a token table.

The Meta Muse Code product page, where the "Models and pricing" section is a Muse Spark token table with no price for the agent itself, as taken from [Meta](https://developer.meta.com/ai/products/muse-code/)

So the real rate card is the Model API rate card. Every model Meta sells, as published on [pricing and rate limits](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits):

Three models, two prices, and no cheap-legacy escape hatch: 1.1 costs exactly what 1.2 costs. Rate limits apply per team rather than per key, so extra keys buy you nothing. Background submissions carry a third cap of 600 per minute on top. If you want the model-side reading of those same numbers, including what changed between 1.1 and 1.2, that is what the [Muse Spark 1.2 pricing](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/meta-muse-spark-12-pricing) breakdown covers.

Then the extras, or rather the lack of them. There is one genuine add-on meter, web search grounding at **$2.50 per 1,000 queries**, charged on top of tokens and flat regardless of how much context each search pulls. Beyond that, Meta has less pricing machinery than most vendors, and mostly in your favour:

*   **No long-context premium.** Meta says it flatly: "There is no long-context premium: you pay the same rate whether your context window is mostly empty or almost full." Several rivals step the price up past a context threshold. Meta does not.
*   **No cache-write fee.** Caching is automatic, cached tokens are a subset of input tokens rather than a separate line, and the optional `"24h"` retention hint costs nothing extra.
*   **Meta's own scaffolding is free.** From the docs: "Meta injects a small amount of steering context into every prompt (a system prompt and related scaffolding); those injected tokens are not billed."
*   **No batch API and no batch discount.** `background: true` responses exist but are not discounted.
*   **No fine-tuning, at any price.** There is no fine-tuning product in the docs at all.
*   **No volume or committed-use discount.** The pricing page's words are "no minimums or upfront commitment," which cuts both ways.

That is an unusually clean rate card. Everything expensive about Muse Code happens somewhere else.

## The three defaults that set your bill

Every metered agent has three or four settings that decide the size of the invoice. What makes Muse Code worth writing about is that all three of its cost dials ship at their expensive position, and none of them is on the pricing page.

![Three dials labelled model, reasoning effort and spend cap, each set to its most expensive position, bracketed together as the out-of-the-box bill](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn-public.eesel.ai%2F314c3443-850d-416d-8721-d2e52c7ac2e2%2F585703e2-5508-4d19-8a3a-24b54e4a1f15%2F0c2c2769b8964933bf111b00cb543509.png&w=1680&q=75)

Three dials labelled model, reasoning effort and spend cap, each set to its most expensive position, bracketed together as the out-of-the-box bill

**Dial one is the model.** Meta's [configuration docs](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/configuration) say it plainly: "The default model is `muse-spark-1.2`." That is the $1.25 and $4.25 tier, not the ten-cent one.

Here is where it gets muddy, and I want to be precise because the gap between the two answers is 12.5x on input. The [launch blog](https://developer.meta.com/ai/resources/blog/build-with-muse-code/) says the opposite: Muse Code "starts on a contributor tier," and it gives you the switch command, `/model to muse-spark-1.2-contributor

# Meta Muse Code Contributor Tier: 20x Off, One Catch

Meta's new terminal coding agent comes with a pricing tier roughly twenty times cheaper than standard, and the price is your prompts and completions. Here is the arithmetic, and who should not take it.

![Cecilia Iona](https://ashyyneusxtubdhsfpod.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/blog-assets/authors/cecilia-iona.png)

[Cecilia Iona](https://swarmz.net/blog/author/cecilia-iona)

Senior Editor, AI & Product

·7 August 2026·1 min read

Meta introduced Muse Code, a terminal coding agent, and the Muse Spark 1.2 model behind it on 5 August 2026. The part worth your attention is not the agent. It is the pricing: alongside standard rates, Meta is offering a Meta Muse Code Contributor tier at a small fraction of the standard price, and the discount is paid for with your prompts and completions, which Meta may use to train future models.

## What Meta actually announced

Per [Meta's own research blog](https://research.meta.ai/blog/introducing-muse-code-and-muse-spark-1-2), Muse Code is a terminal coding agent in beta that plans, writes and validates changes across large repositories, with background agents and a local event log. Muse Spark 1.2 is the coding-focused model powering it, available in Muse Code and the Meta Model API. [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2231285/meta-introduces-muse-code-its-take-on-a-coding-agent) and [MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/2026/08/05/meta-muse-code-for-mac/) both put availability at macOS and Linux at launch.

Reporting across those outlets puts standard API pricing at roughly $1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 per million output tokens, with the Contributor tier around $0.10 input and $0.20 output. That is a discount of roughly 12x on input and 20x on output. The Contributor tier is also described as carrying materially lower rate limits than standard.

## The trade, stated plainly

You are not buying a cheaper model. You are buying the same model at a lower price by granting permission for your prompts and completions to be used to improve Meta's models. For a coding agent, prompts and completions means your source code, your file paths, your error messages, and whatever you happened to paste into the terminal while debugging.
